query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Coating high-entropy alloy (HEA) components with a thin, uniform layer of 2D HEA nanoflakes (e.g. of (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 composition) will trigger in situ tribocatalytic reactions during sliding that form a lubricious amorphous carbon tribolayer, thereby reducing both the coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: A bulk high-entropy alloy component with its typical microstructure and without any integrated self‐lubricating surface treatment.
generation.intervention: Apply a uniform spray coating of 2D HEA nanoflakes onto the component’s contact surfaces.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted in ambient conditions (with trace hydrocarbons/ethanol residues available) and over an extended temperature range (from room temperature up to moderately high temperatures below the decomposition threshold of the coating).
generation.structural_mediator: In situ formation of an amorphous carbon (a‐C) tribolayer on the surface mediated by the catalytic activity of the 2D nanoflakes.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, the catalytically active 2D HEA nanoflakes dissociate entrapped ethanol or other organic molecules, leading to the formation of an a‐C tribofilm. This lubricious layer reduces shear forces at the interface and minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact, thus lowering both friction and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to uncoated HEA components, the spray‐coated components are expected to show a significant drop in friction coefficient (potentially a 20–30% or greater reduction) and an order-of-magnitude improvement in wear rate.
generation.baseline: The untreated HEA component under identical tribological testing conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect relies on the availability of trace organic species (e.g. ethanol) to serve as carbon sources; performance may be compromised in environments devoid of such vapors or at temperatures exceeding the thermal stability of the nanoflake coating.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of friction and wear reductions is uncertain and may depend on the coating’s uniformity, the specific operating temperature, and the ambient organic content.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of identical HEA samples. One group is spray-coated with the 2D HEA nanoflake layer (e.g. (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2) while the control group remains uncoated. Subject both sets to standardized ball-on-disk tribological tests over a range of temperatures (e.g. from room temperature up to 600 °C) in ambient air with controlled trace organic vapor concentrations.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (measured continuously during sliding)
Tribofilm presence, thickness, and composition (via Raman spectroscopy and SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction (e.g., less than 20% lower friction coefficient and no notable improvement in wear rate compared to controls) or if no amorphous carbon tribolayer is detected on the wear track, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To comprehend the lubricious behavior of the 2D HEA, it is important to understand the tribochemical reactions occurring during the friction test. The evolution of surface morphology and elemental analysis of the wear tracks was carried out on the post‐test disk by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Table S1, Supporting Information) and Raman spectroscopy (Figure 3a; Figure S4, Supporting Information). From both SEM and optical imaging, the debris was found at the center and near the edge of the wear tracks, which signifies the formation and sweeping away of the tribolayer at the contact area. From the Raman spectroscopy performed on the wear tracks, besides the peaks corresponding to HEA flakes (351 cm−1 and 416 cm−1), there is a presence of two more strong peaks at 1370 cm−1 and 1590 cm−1, which correspond to D‐peak and G‐peak of carbon, respectively. The tribofilm was found to contain HEA flakes and some amorphous carbon (a‐carbon, a‐C) that was formed during the test as observed from the Raman results (Figure S4, Supporting Information). Previous tribological studies in the liquid environment using oil and other hydrocarbons as lubricating mediums have reported the formation of carbon tribofilms as well. In these studies, the abundance of long‐chain hydrocarbons, like olefin oil, present around the tribocatalytic metal coatings act as the carbon sources for the carbon film formation reaction during the sliding process.[ , , ,  ] However, in the current work, the 2D HEA nanoflakes acted as the solid lubricant with residues of ethanol available for the tribocatalytic reaction. In this case, the high catalytic activity of (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 nanoflakes plays a critical role in the formation of an a‐C tribolayer and substantial reduction in friction.

Intrigued by the extensive lubricious behavior of the HEA in ethanol, a further study has been conducted to analyze the capabilities of HEA nanoflakes in other solvents like water. The (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 powder is combined with distilled water at a concentration of 1.5g L−1. This water‐based lubricant solution was sonicated for thorough mixing (≈9 h sonication time) and spray coated uniformly onto the steel disk for ball‐on‐disk friction experiments across all loads from 1 N to 9 N. The results found all sliding tests to fail within short distances (Figure S5, Supporting Information). In Figure S5 (Supporting Information), the starting COF decreases with an increase in load, showing the intrinsic HEA behavior like in the case of HEA in ethanol. However, the HEA in water exhibits limited wear resistance and high wear rates in the magnitude of 10−6 mm3 (N∙m)−1 as compared to HEA in ethanol which has wear rates in the magnitude of 10−9 mm3 (N∙m)−1. This shows that the ethanol solvent plays a significant role in increasing the tribological performance of HEA during friction tests. In summary, we developed a novel solid lubricant based on the 2D HEA structure, which combines the advantages of HEAs enhanced mechanical properties and low‐shearing behavior of 2D materials to demonstrate a superior self‐lubricating behavior. The comprehensive post‐test characterizations coupled with MD simulation studies revealed interesting tribochemistry at play leading to the dissociation of entrapped ethanol molecules and converting it into a‐C in the presence of catalytically active HEA nanoflakes, which are responsible for the formation of tribolayer, wherein the full lubricious behavior was complemented by the retained HEA nanoflakes. This discovery opens up a new avenue to develop advanced solid lubricants based on 2D HEA with high compositional flexibility and low‐shear‐strength layered structure for oil‐free tribological systems. The other important aspect of the 2D HEA lubricant developed in this study is the ability to coat the given surface using a simple spray coating technique.
